"Lineal" describes something that exists in a direct, unbroken line of descent — meaning it relates to the straight-line connection from an ancestor down through their child, that child's child, and so on, generation after generation.

When you call someone a lineal descendant of another person, you are saying that the connection between them runs in a straight, vertical line through a family tree — with no sideways jumps through siblings or cousins. It is the path that goes directly from great-great-grandmother → great-grandmother → grandmother → parent → you.
Understanding "Direct Line" with a Simple Picture

Imagine drawing a family tree on paper. You are at the bottom. Your parents are one step above you. Their parents are one step above them. Keep going up, and you trace a straight, vertical line all the way back through the centuries.

That straight vertical line — going directly upward — is your lineal line. Every person on that line above you is your lineal ancestor. Every person on that line below you — your children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren — is your lineal descendant.

The word "lineal" is essentially about this straight, vertical line in a family tree. Nothing more, nothing less.
The Most Important Contrast: Lineal vs. Collateral

This contrast is the heart of the word, and understanding it will make everything click.

Not all relatives are lineal. Relatives who are not on that straight vertical line are called collateral relatives. A collateral relative shares a common ancestor with you, but they branch off to the side of your family tree — they are not directly above or below you.

Your parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents are lineal ancestors. Your children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren are lineal descendants. But your siblings, cousins, aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews — while they are your relatives — are collateral, not lineal. They did not come directly from you, and you did not come directly from them. The line between you and them is not a straight vertical drop; it goes sideways first.

A simple test: to get from your great-grandmother to you, does the path pass through a sibling or a cousin? No. It goes straight down. Great-grandmother had a child, that child had a child, that child had you. No detours. That is what makes it lineal.
Lineal vs. Linear — Don't Confuse These Two

"Lineal" and "linear" look nearly identical and share the same roots, but in modern English they mean different things and are used in completely different contexts.

Linear is a broad, everyday word meaning "of or relating to a line" in a very general sense. You use it in mathematics (a linear equation), in descriptions of thinking or progress (linear reasoning, linear growth), or to describe something arranged in a straight physical line.

Lineal, by contrast, is a narrow, specialized word used almost exclusively to talk about lines of descent and ancestry. You would never describe a road or a math problem as "lineal." You would only use it when talking about family, bloodlines, and inheritance.

The practical rule is simple: if the topic is ancestry, family descent, or inheritance, use lineal. For everything else — mathematics, shapes, sequences, thinking — use linear.
Where You Will Actually See "Lineal" Used

Because "lineal" is specifically about family descent, you will encounter it most often in three areas.

In law, "lineal" is used constantly in wills, estate planning, and inheritance disputes. A will might specify that a property is to go to the deceased person's "lineal descendants," which means only their direct children and grandchildren qualify — not their siblings' children or their cousins. Courts also use "lineal heir" to define who has a legitimate claim to inherit a title, estate, or asset through direct family descent.

In genealogy, researchers use "lineal" to describe the direct-line ancestors they are tracing. Someone might say they have traced their lineal ancestry back eight generations, meaning they followed the strict, unbroken parent-to-child chain backward in time.

In history and anthropology, scholars describe societies by how they organize lineal descent — some cultures trace family identity and inheritance through the mother's lineal line (matrilineal), others through the father's (patrilineal).

The word "lineal" rarely appears alone. Here are the phrases you will most often see it in, along with what each one means.

Lineal descendant — a person who descends directly from another through an unbroken parent-to-child chain. Your child is your lineal descendant. So is your grandchild, and every generation below them.

Lineal ancestor — a person from whom you descend directly. Your parent, grandparent, and great-grandparent are your lineal ancestors.

Lineal heir — in law, the person who inherits through the direct line of descent, not through a sideways branch of the family.

Lineal succession — the passing of a throne, title, or estate in a straight line from parent to child, generation after generation.

"She was confirmed as a lineal descendant of the founding king, her ancestry tracing directly from father to daughter across twelve generations."

"The estate was left only to his lineal descendants — his two children and four grandchildren — with his cousins and siblings receiving nothing."

"The tribe's oral history recognized only lineal male heirs as eligible to lead, requiring an unbroken father-to-son chain all the way back to the first chief."

"After centuries of collateral succession, the crown finally returned to a lineal heir."
A Rare, Secondary Meaning Worth Knowing

A handful of older dictionaries also list "lineal" as meaning "of, relating to, or consisting of lines" in a general, visual sense — as in describing something made up of lines. This use is extremely rare today and considered archaic. You are very unlikely to encounter it, and you should never feel the need to use it yourself. Whenever you see "lineal" in any modern text, it almost certainly refers to the genealogical meaning described above.

Lineal means directly in the line of descent — connected through an unbroken, straight chain of parent to child, as opposed to through a sideways family branch like siblings, cousins, or other collateral relatives.
